title: Claim Element Mapping in Patent Invalidity: Building a Reference-by-Reference Strategy (practitioner methodology write-up)

extracted.subtask_short: Operational rubric: segment, pin down meaning, quote, cite precisely
extracted.subtask_description: A practitioner-level operational rubric for building a single-reference anticipation claim mapping: parse elements before searching, fix claim meaning via specification/prosecution/construction order, target the hardest elements first, and require quoted, precisely-cited, explained correspondence rather than a holistic similarity narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parse the claim into numbered elements before touching prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: "Read each claim slowly and divide it into its individual limitations." Use the claim's own punctuation and connective language (";", "wherein", "comprising", "further comprising") as natural breakpoints between limitations. Number each resulting element explicitly (element 1, element 2, ...) — this numbering becomes the backbone of the eventual claim chart. This maps directly onto the "each and every element" doctrine in MPEP § 2131: the parsing step operationalizes what counts as "an element" for the purposes of checking single-reference disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine or lump together similar-sounding elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and patent tribunals construe claims narrowly and expect each limitation to be individually accounted for; conflating two limitations into one row of analysis is a common and consequential charting error, because a reference might satisfy one but not the other of two elements that were wrongly merged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the claim's meaning before searching for art
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding whether a reference "discloses" a limitation, consult, in order: (1) the specification (for any explicit definitions or lexicography the patentee gave to a claim term); (2) the prosecution history (for narrowing arguments/amendments the applicant made to secure allowance — these can estop broader readings later); (3) any existing claim construction order (in litigation contexts, a court's construction is controlling and must be used as the operative meaning, not a practitioner's own reading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key preparatory questions: Did the patentee define a claim term explicitly? Did the applicant make narrowing arguments to distinguish prior art during prosecution — arguments that now bind the scope available for a corresponding invalidity mapping? Does the limitation include functional language subject to a broad or narrow construction (connects to MPEP § 2114's capability-based reading of functional apparatus limitations)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Search prior art targeting the hardest/most specific elements first
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize search terms drawn from the claim's most technically specific limitations — generic/broad limitations are easy to find in almost any reference and provide little discriminating power; the specific limitations narrow the useful candidate-reference set fastest. Cast a wide net across patent databases (USPTO, EPO, WIPO, Google Patents) and non-patent literature (academic papers, product manuals, conference proceedings, datasheets) — anticipatory references are not limited to patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary filter: does the reference cover at least three or four claim elements?
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a quick preliminary filter to any candidate reference: "can this reference cover at least three or four of the claim elements?" References that only plausibly cover one or two elements are unlikely to be single-reference anticipatory candidates and are better reserved for an obviousness combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote the reference directly and explain terminology differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote the reference directly, rather than paraphrasing or summarizing what it says. If the reference uses different terminology than the claim, the chart must not simply assert a match — it must explain the correspondence explicitly, articulating why the differently-worded disclosure describes the same structure or function as the claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practitioner-level operationalization of the *In re Bond* "not an ipsissimis verbis test" rule from MPEP 2131 — same substance, different words, is permissible, but the burden is on the chart-builder to show the equivalence, not merely assert it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations must be precise — column/line, paragraph, or figure references
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations must be precise: column and line numbers, specific paragraph numbers, or specific figure references — not vague pointers like "see generally column 3." A chart that cannot point to the specific textual/graphical location supporting a mapped element is treated as inadequate disclosure, regardless of whether the underlying reference might actually support the mapping somewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, traceable correspondence required per element (no overall narrative substitute)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chart must show "a direct, traceable correspondence between the claim language and the prior art disclosure" for each individual element — an overall narrative of similarity is not a substitute for element-level traceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common charting pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping to an outdated or superseded claim version (e.g., analyzing claims as originally filed when they were later amended during prosecution); vague or general citations that don't pinpoint the exact disclosure location; ignoring dependent claims (each adds its own limitation(s) that must be separately mapped); disregarding claim construction orders where one already exists; failing to map each element individually (reverting to a holistic "this reference basically shows the same invention" argument instead of the required limitation-by-limitation showing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational rubric summary for a claim-matching system
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations must first be segmented into a canonical, numbered list (the "ground truth" set of things that need matching) — this segmentation step itself is a place where systems/analysts can introduce error (over- or under-segmenting). A claim term's meaning must be pinned down (via internal definitions, prosecution history, or construction) before any matching decision is made. A match is only "real" if it is (a) specific — cited to a particular location/passage in the reference, and (b) explained — especially when wording differs, the correspondence in substance must be articulated, not simply asserted. A single reference should ideally be evaluated against most/all elements before being treated as a serious anticipation candidate (rough heuristic: at least 3-4 of the claim's elements); weak partial matches belong to the separate obviousness analysis, not anticipation.
